query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled post-deposition annealing of a FeNiCrCoCu thin coating induces Cu segregation to the surface, forming a lubricious, Cu‐rich interlayer (or modified oxide) that reduces direct metal–metal contact during high-temperature sliding and thereby decreases the wear rate while promoting more ductile, shear‐dominated microscopic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment (at a temperature high enough to promote diffusion but below melting, e.g. 300–400°C for a specified duration) to drive Cu segregation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear regime (approximately 300–400°C) under controlled load and sliding speed.
generation.structural_mediator: A Cu-rich surface layer and/or associated modified oxide film that forms as a result of thermally activated Cu diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature during annealing enhances Cu mobility in the FeNiCrCoCu alloy, leading to its segregation at the surface. This segregated Cu-rich phase acts as a lubricious interlayer that lowers interfacial shear during sliding, thereby reducing friction and wear. In parallel, the altered surface chemistry changes the microscopic deformation from brittle cracking to a more ductile mode dominated by dislocation glide and shear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an as-deposited baseline, the annealed coating will exhibit a lowered coefficient of friction and reduced wear volume during high-temperature sliding. Microscopic analysis is expected to reveal enhanced Cu enrichment at the surface, along with evidence of ductile shear deformation rather than brittle cracking.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating without any post-deposition heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (near 300–400°C) where sufficient thermal activation enables Cu diffusion; at lower temperatures, insufficient Cu migration may preclude formation of the lubricious phase.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Cu segregation, its spatial distribution, and the relative contributions of any subsequent oxide formation versus pure metallic segregation in reducing wear are not fully quantified and require detailed microstructural and tribological studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples on identical metal substrates. One set remains as-deposited (baseline) and the other is subjected to the prescribed annealing treatment. Conduct sliding wear tests at 300–400°C under identical loads and sliding speeds. Post-test, perform surface and cross-sectional characterization (e.g., SEM, EDS) to assess Cu distribution and examine the deformed microstructures.
measurements: Wear volume or wear rate of the coating
Microstructural analysis of the wear track (e.g., presence and extent of Cu-rich phase)
Evaluation of deformation features (e.g., evidence of ductile shear vs. brittle cracking)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear rate compared to the as-deposited baseline, and if microstructural analysis fails to reveal evidence of Cu enrichment at the surface or a change in the deformation mechanism, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening.
